cite_as: Lee, V. E., & Burkam, D. T. (2001). Dropping out of high school: The role of school organization and structure (ERIC ED458694; later in American Educational Research Journal 40(2), 2003)
claimed_finding: Longitudinal multilevel study of 3,840 students in 190 high schools (NELS:88): students in schools with more positive student-teacher relations were less likely to drop out between grades 10 and 12, controlling for grade 10 math achievement and background; the association held only in small and medium public and Catholic schools, not in large schools

cite_as: Barile, Donohue, Anthony, Baker, Weaver & Henrich (2012). Teacher-student relationship climate and school outcomes: Implications for educational policy initiatives. Journal of Youth and Adolescence 41(3), 256-267
claimed_finding: Longitudinal multilevel model of 7,779 students in 431 public high schools (ELS:2002): a more positive school teacher-student relationship climate was associated with lower dropout by senior year, controlling for sophomore math scores and background; it was not significantly associated with math achievement gains

cite_as: Gubbels, van der Put & Assink (2019). Risk factors for school absenteeism and dropout: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Youth and Adolescence 48(9), 1637-1667
claimed_finding: Meta-analysis of unadjusted associations: poor pupil-teacher relationship is a significant risk factor for absenteeism (r about .29) but only a non-significant trend for dropout (r about .13)

cite_as: Allensworth & Easton (2007). What matters for staying on-track and graduating in Chicago Public High Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research
claimed_finding: Chicago ninth graders in schools with high versus low student-reported teacher-student trust had about 2.3 fewer days of absence per semester, controlling for eighth-grade test scores and background (not prior attendance)

cite_as: Hamlin (2021). Can a positive school climate promote student attendance? Evidence from New York City. American Educational Research Journal 58(2), 315-342
claimed_finding: New York City grades 6-12 (about 824,000 students): student-reported climate measures had only small associations with attendance, and changes in climate were only marginally associated with attendance

cite_as: Roorda, Koomen, Spilt & Oort (2011). The influence of affective teacher-student relationships on students' school engagement and achievement: A meta-analytic approach. Review of Educational Research 81(4)
claimed_finding: Meta-analysis of 99 studies pooling zero-order correlations (r about .16 for positive relationships and achievement); the authors state the zero-order correlations may overestimate unique effects, with no adjustment for prior achievement

cite_as: Roorda, Jak, Zee, Oort & Koomen (2017). Affective teacher-student relationships and students' engagement and achievement: A meta-analytic update. School Psychology Review 46(3)
claimed_finding: Meta-analytic update of 189 studies: engagement partly mediates the relationship-achievement association; the authors say most studies were cross-sectional and the data do not permit conclusions about causality; no prior-achievement covariate

cite_as: Hughes, Im & Allee (2015). Effect of school belonging trajectories in grades 6-8 on achievement: Gender and ethnic differences. Journal of School Psychology 53(6)
claimed_finding: Longitudinal study of 527 academically at-risk Texas students: grade 6 school belonging predicted grade 8 reading and math slightly (coefficients about .05 to .10) above grade 5 achievement
